\chapter{Greetings}
\label{ch:greetings}
\hlchaptermodality{1}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can greet someone, say yes, no and thank you, agree with sari, hold a short exchange out loud, and copy my first Tamil shape with a visible model.}

Hold the whole exchange out loud, then copy \ta{வ} once beside the visible model and compare only that shape.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[vaṇakkam]{\ta{வணக்கம்} (vaṇakkam) — \textquotedblleft{}greetings\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TA-C01-vanakkam}



\begin{quote}
The first Tamil word, and the one you will use most. One word, one lesson. Say it, and you have greeted someone.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{வணக்கம்}}
\textbf{\ta{வணக்கம்}} — \emph{vaṇakkam} — \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}greetings.\textquotedblright{}}

Say it \emph{va-ṇak-kam}, with the \emph{kk} held a beat longer than a single \emph{k}.

It is what you say walking into a room, answering a phone, or meeting anyone at all. It does not change for morning or evening, and it does not change for one person or many.

\begin{quote}
Its root is the verb \emph{vaṇaṅku}, \textquotedblleft{}to bow.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Vaṇakkam} is the act of bowing, turned into a word — and it is native Tamil, not borrowed from Sanskrit.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
Say it \emph{va-ṇak-kam}. The ṇ is a \textbf{retroflex} \emph{n} — curl the tongue back to the roof of the mouth, further back than an English \emph{n}. The \emph{kk} is \textbf{held}, a beat longer than a single \emph{k}, and that length is doing real work: Tamil distinguishes words by it.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ta{வணக்கம்}} (\emph{vaṇakkam}) comes from the verb \emph{vaṇaṅku}, “to bow, to pay homage.” Turned into a noun of the action, it means “a bowing, an act of reverence” — the idea of \emph{namaste}, but from a \textbf{native Tamil} root, not a Sanskrit one. That is Tamil's whole personality: an old language that keeps its home-grown words where its neighbours borrowed.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Said with the palms pressed together and a small bow — the gesture \emph{is} the word. It serves as both \textbf{hello and goodbye}, any time, to almost anyone, respectful without being stiff.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Writing — let your finger meet one shape}
Keep \textbf{\ta{வணக்கம்}} visible. Find only its first shape: \textbf{\ta{வ}}. Follow that printed shape once with your finger while you say the whole greeting.

Do not write it yet, and do not try to remember the whole word. This first pass only lets your eye, voice, and hand notice the same greeting together. A later script lesson will teach how Tamil letters are formed; tracing a typeface here does not claim a handwriting stroke order.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vaṇakkam\textquotedblright{} — hold the \emph{kk}
  \item it to someone arriving
  \item it to someone leaving — the same word does both
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textbf{\ta{வணக்கம்}}. Does it change between morning and evening? (\textbf{No} — one greeting, all day.) Does it change for one person or a crowd? (\textbf{No}.) Next: the same greeting across the Dravidian family.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[va]{\ta{வ} (va) — copy one visible shape with help}

\label{lesson:TA-W00-va-guided-copy}



\begin{quote}
Point to \textbf{\ta{வணக்கம்}} and say \emph{vaṇakkam} once. Keep the model on the page. Find the first shape, \textbf{\ta{வ}} (\emph{va}), which your finger just followed.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — one supported copy}
Copy \textbf{\ta{வ}} once beside the model. Look back as often as you need. Your copy can be large and slow; it does not need to look like a font.

This is shape familiarity, not a stroke-order test. Do not hide the model, do not copy the rest of \textbf{\ta{வணக்கம்}}, and do not add a second new shape today. The later Tamil writing sequence will teach letter construction explicitly.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Compare your one copy with \textbf{\ta{வ}} (\emph{va}) while both remain visible. Repair one curve if you want, then stop. Say \emph{vaṇakkam} once more: one known greeting, one tiny hand movement.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vaṇakkam / namaskāram]{\ta{வணக்கம்} — one bow, two lexical loyalties}

\label{lesson:TA-C01-vanakkam-family-register}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Vaṇakkam} names a bow. Neighboring languages name the same gesture with a different inherited or borrowed root.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Hello\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{Source} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Tamil} & \emph{vaṇakkam} & \textbf{native Dravidian} \emph{vaṇaṅku} \\
Kannada & \emph{namaskāra} & Sanskrit \\
Telugu & \emph{namaskāram} & Sanskrit \\
Malayalam & \emph{namaskāram} & Sanskrit \\
Hindi & \emph{namaste} & Sanskrit \\
English & \emph{hello} & Germanic hailing-call \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Four tracks use Sanskrit \emph{namas-}, \textquotedblleft{}bow.\textquotedblright{} Tamil kept its own verb. The gesture and social meaning match; the lexical loyalty differs.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Say \emph{vaṇakkam} with pressed palms or a small head-bow: the gesture is the word. It works as \textbf{hello and goodbye}, at any time, to almost anyone. It is respectful without being stiff; cinema and formal speech can also use it as a ringing one-word salutation to a whole room.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}vaṇakkam\textquotedblright{} with a small bow
  \item \emph{Contrast:} Tamil \emph{vaṇaṅku} · neighbors Sanskrit \emph{namas-}
  \item \emph{Choose:} greeting or parting $\to$ \textbf{\ta{வணக்கம்}} works
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Dravidian language kept its native bow-word? (\textbf{Tamil}.) What did the neighbors borrow? (Sanskrit \emph{\textbf{namas-}}.) Can \emph{vaṇakkam} greet and part? (\textbf{Yes} — it is an all-day respectful salutation.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ām]{\ta{ஆம்} (ām) — \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TA-C01-aam}



\begin{quote}
The plain yes. One word, and then we will put these together.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{ஆம்}}
\textbf{\ta{ஆம்}} — \emph{ām} — \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}yes.\textquotedblright{}}

One beat, with a long opening \emph{aa}.

Stretch it and you get \emph{\textbf{āmām}} — \textquotedblleft{}yes, indeed; that's right.\textquotedblright{} Tamil doubles words for warmth and certainty, the way \emph{sari sari} does.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Ām} is a worn-down form of \emph{āgum}, \textquotedblleft{}it becomes, it will be\textquotedblright{} — a yes that started life as a verb, which is a very Tamil way to agree.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
Say it \emph{ām} — a \textbf{long} \emph{a}, held about twice as long as the short one, closing on a plain \emph{m}. Vowel length is meaningful in Tamil, so the length is not decoration.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ta{ஆம்}} (\emph{ām}) is the plain “yes.” Doubled for emphasis it becomes \emph{āmām}, “yes, indeed.”
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens}]
Tamil often says “yes” by \textbf{echoing the verb}: asked \emph{vandāyā?} (“did you come?”), a natural yes is \emph{vandēṉ} (“I came”). Bank \emph{ām} as the simple word, but expect a “yes” to come back as a whole verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ām\textquotedblright{} — one long \emph{aa}, closed on the \emph{m}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āmām\textquotedblright{} — the emphatic double
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ām\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}sari\textquotedblright{} — yes, and alright
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textbf{\ta{ஆம்}}. What does \emph{\textbf{āmām}} add? (\textbf{Emphasis} — \textquotedblleft{}yes, indeed.\textquotedblright{}) Next: the word for no.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[illai]{\ta{இல்லை} (illai) — \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TA-C01-illai}



\begin{quote}
The other half of the pair. One word, and then the lesson that puts all five together.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{இல்லை}}
\textbf{\ta{இல்லை}} — \emph{illai} — \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}no.\textquotedblright{}}

Two beats: \emph{il-lai}, with the \emph{l} held across the join.

On its own it is the everyday \textbf{no}. But it is not really the adjective \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} — it is a small statement meaning \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}is not.\textquotedblright{}} That will matter when we put the five words together.

\begin{quote}
Its root is \emph{il}, the idea of \emph{not-being}. Its positive twin is \emph{uṇḍu}, \textquotedblleft{}there is.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
Say it \emph{il-lai}, with the \emph{l} \textbf{held} across the join — the same doubling you met in \emph{vaṇak-kam}. The ending is the diphthong \emph{ai}, as in English “eye,” not two separate vowels.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\ta{இல்லை} (\emph{illai}) is built on \ta{இல்} (\emph{il}), “not-being, absence” — so it is not really the adjective “no” but the statement \textbf{“{[}it{]} is not, {[}there{]} is not.”} Its positive twin is \emph{uṇḍu}, “there is.”
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens}]
\textbf{Tamil negates by \emph{being}, not with a “not”-word.} Where English inserts \emph{not}/\emph{no}, Tamil swaps in the negative verb of existence: \emph{puttakam \textbf{uṇḍu}} (“there \emph{is} a book”) $\to$ \emph{puttakam \textbf{illai}} (“there \emph{is not} a book”). So \emph{illai} is both the everyday “no” and the word that makes a whole sentence negative — a deeply Dravidian habit, unlike English or Hindi.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}illai\textquotedblright{} — two beats, the \emph{l} held across the join
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}ām\textquotedblright{} … \textquotedblleft{}illai\textquotedblright{}
  \item it alone, as a complete answer
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textbf{\ta{இல்லை}}. Is it closer to English \emph{no}, or to \emph{is not}? (\textbf{Is not} — it is a statement, not a label.) Next: the word for thank you.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[naṉṟi]{\ta{நன்றி} (naṉṟi) — \textquotedblleft{}thank you\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TA-C01-nandri}



\begin{quote}
One word again. This is the one you will reach for second-most, and Tamil says it with a noun rather than a verb.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{நன்றி}}
\textbf{\ta{நன்றி}} — \emph{naṉṟi} — \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}thank you.\textquotedblright{}}

Two beats: \emph{naṉ-ṟi}. The \emph{ṉ} and the \emph{ṟ} are both made further back than English \emph{n} and \emph{r}; copy the sound rather than the spelling.

It works on its own, with no verb around it. Someone hands you something; you say \emph{naṉṟi}, and that is a whole sentence.

\begin{quote}
Its root is \emph{nal}, \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} — the same \emph{nal-} inside \emph{nalla} (\textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{nanmai} (\textquotedblleft{}a good deed\textquotedblright{}). Saying \emph{naṉṟi} names the good someone did you.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
Say it \emph{naṉ-ṟi}. Tamil hears \textbf{three} different \emph{n} sounds and this word uses two of them: a \textbf{dental} \emph{n} (tongue on the teeth) to open, then an \textbf{alveolar} \emph{ṉ} (on the ridge just behind them). The \emph{ṟ} is its own sound again, not the English \emph{r}. English ears flatten all of this to “nandri,” which is close enough to be understood.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ta{நன்றி}} (\emph{naṉṟi}) grows from the root \emph{nal}, “good” — so it literally means \textbf{“goodness.”} To thank, in Tamil, is to name the good someone did you.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens}]
\textbf{Tamil hears three of every \emph{n}, \emph{l}, and \emph{r}.} You have now heard two of the three \emph{n}s inside this one word: a dental \emph{n} (tongue on the teeth) and an alveolar \emph{ṉ} (on the ridge behind them). There is a third, the retroflex \emph{ṇ} you met in \emph{vaṇakkam} — curled back. Tamil does the same for \emph{l} (\emph{l}, \emph{ḷ}, \emph{ḻ}) and for \emph{r} (\emph{r}, \emph{ṟ}). English fuses each set into one letter; Tamil keeps them apart, and the differences \emph{change meaning}.

Each of those sounds has its own letter, and you will meet the letters one at a time later, spelling words you already say. Learn the sounds word by word, not as a chart.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}naṉṟi\textquotedblright{} — two beats, both consonants far back
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vaṇakkam\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}naṉṟi\textquotedblright{} — greeting, then thanks
  \item it on its own, with nothing around it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textbf{\ta{நன்றி}}. Does it need a verb to be a complete reply? (\textbf{No} — it stands alone.) Next: how thanks travels across the family.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[naṉṟi / nandi]{\ta{நன்றி} — a native family word with a register edge}

\label{lesson:TA-C01-nandri-family-register}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Naṉṟi} literally names goodness. Its family distribution mirrors the greeting split you just saw.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Thanks\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{Source} \\
\midrule
\textbf{Tamil} & \emph{naṉṟi} & native \emph{nal}, \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} \\
Malayalam & \emph{nandi} & the \textbf{same Dravidian word} \\
Kannada & \emph{dhanyavāda} & Sanskrit \\
Telugu & \emph{dhanyavādamulu} & Sanskrit \\
Hindi & \emph{dhanyavād / shukriyā} & Sanskrit / Perso-Arabic \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Tamil and its closest sister Malayalam kept the native word. Kannada and Telugu borrowed Sanskrit \emph{dhanyavāda}, repeating the split seen with \textquotedblleft{}hello.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Spoken \emph{naṉṟi} can feel a little formal. Everyday warmth may live in a smile or nod; among close family an explicit thank-you can sound oddly distant. Use \textbf{romba naṉṟi}, \textquotedblleft{}many thanks,\textquotedblright{} when you want to mark gratitude strongly.

This is a register tendency, not a ban: the relationship and moment determine whether naming the gratitude feels warm or ceremonious.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} Tamil \emph{naṉṟi} · Malayalam \emph{nandi}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}romba naṉṟi\textquotedblright{} — many thanks
  \item \emph{Choose:} close-family routine favor $\to$ warmth may be nonverbal
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which sister shares Tamil's native gratitude word? (\textbf{Malayalam}.) What did Kannada and Telugu borrow? (Sanskrit \emph{\textbf{dhanyavāda}}.) Why can explicit \emph{naṉṟi} sound marked? (Among intimates, gratitude may be assumed; the word can feel \textbf{formal}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sari]{\ta{சரி} (sari) — \textquotedblleft{}okay\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TA-C01-sari}



\begin{quote}
The most useful small word in the language, and the easiest to say.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{சரி}}
\textbf{\ta{சரி}} — \emph{sari} — \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}okay, alright, correct.\textquotedblright{}}

Two beats: \emph{sa-ri}.

It is the verbal nod of Tamil. Someone proposes a plan and the whole reply is one warm \emph{sari}. Doubled — \emph{sari, sari} — it means \textquotedblleft{}yes yes, fine, go on.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{quote}
It began as \textquotedblleft{}correct, even, level,\textquotedblright{} and slid from \emph{that is right} to \emph{alright} the way English \emph{right} did.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
Say it \emph{sari}, two light syllables, stress even. The opening sound sits between English \emph{s} and \emph{ch}, and Tamil treats that whole range as one sound chosen by \textbf{position} in the word rather than by a separate spelling — the same economy that lets one \emph{k}-sound also be heard as \emph{g} or a soft \emph{h}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\ta{சரி} (\emph{sari}) is native Tamil for “correct, even, level,” and so “okay, agreed.” It is the verbal nod of the language: propose a plan, hear a warm \emph{sari}; doubled, \emph{sari sari} = “alright, alright.”
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens}]
\textbf{One letter, several sounds.} For its stop-consonants Tamil writes \emph{one} letter per mouth-position and lets rules of position fill in the voicing (\emph{k}/\emph{g}, \emph{s}/\emph{ch}). The payoff is a strikingly \emph{small} alphabet; the price is that the exact sound isn't always predictable from the letter alone — you pick it up by ear, word by word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sari\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sari, sari\textquotedblright{} — the doubled, hurry-along version
  \item agree to something with nothing but this word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textbf{\ta{சரி}}. What does doubling it add? (\textbf{Hurry, or easy agreement} — \textquotedblleft{}yes yes, fine.\textquotedblright{}) Next: putting the five words together.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ām / illai / sari]{Putting the five together — how Tamil answers}

\label{lesson:TA-C01-answering}



\begin{quote}
Five words, one at a time. Now they go into a conversation, and two habits show up that English does not have.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange — built from the five words}
A whole exchange, built only from the five words:

\begin{quote}
— \emph{\textbf{vaṇakkam\emph{.\textbf{ — }}vaṇakkam\emph{.\textbf{ — }}sari\emph{?\textbf{ — }}ām\emph{.\textbf{ — }}naṉṟi\emph{.\textbf{ — }}sari\emph{.\textbf{}}}}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{— Hello. — Hello.} \emph{— Alright? — Yes.} \emph{— Thank you. — Alright.}
\end{quote}

Every reply is one word. Tamil is comfortable with that in a way English is not.

Say the exchange, don't read it. Each of these five words is printed in Tamil in its own lesson, and the letters arrive later, one at a time.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two habits behind the answers}]
\textbf{One — Tamil often answers by echoing the verb.}

\emph{Ām} is correct, but a speaker will often say yes by \textbf{repeating the verb of the question}. Asked \textquotedblleft{}did you come?\textquotedblright{}, a natural yes is \emph{vandēṉ} — \textquotedblleft{}I came.\textquotedblright{} Keep \emph{ām} as your word, and expect a yes to come back as a whole verb.

\textbf{Two — Tamil negates by \emph{being}, not with a \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{}-word.}

English makes a sentence negative by inserting \emph{not}. Tamil swaps in the negative verb of existence:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{puttakam \textbf{uṇḍu}} & \textquotedblleft{}there \textbf{is} a book\textquotedblright{} \\
\emph{puttakam \textbf{illai}} & \textquotedblleft{}there \textbf{is not} a book\textquotedblright{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \emph{illai} does double duty: alone it is the everyday \textbf{no}; inside a sentence it is what makes the whole thing negative. Learn it as \emph{is not} and both uses fall out.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the exchange above, both parts
  \item \emph{Hear:} \textquotedblleft{}puttakam uṇḍu\textquotedblright{} … \textquotedblleft{}puttakam illai\textquotedblright{} — only the last word changed
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give a one-word reply to \emph{sari?} and to \emph{naṉṟi}. (\textbf{ām} / \textbf{sari}.) Besides \emph{ām}, what else is a natural yes? (\textbf{Repeating the verb}.) What does \emph{illai} do inside a sentence? (\textbf{Makes it negative} — it is the \textquotedblleft{}is not\textquotedblright{} verb.) Next: the chapter's own recap, and then names.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 1 — a five-word recap}

\label{lesson:TA-C01-practice}



\begin{quote}
Five spoken words, plus the one visible shape your hand has copied. Let's gather only what you have already learned and make it feel easy.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — say them back}]
Say each one before you check the meaning:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Say this} & \textbf{Meaning} \\
\midrule
\emph{vaṇakkam} & hello / greetings \\
\emph{naṉṟi} & thank you \\
\emph{ām} & yes \\
\emph{illai} & no / there isn't \\
\emph{sari} & okay / correct \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

These are five spoken words, so the recap gives you the sound and nothing to decode. One shape is the exception, because it is the one your hand has already met: \textbf{\ta{வணக்கம்}}, whose opening \textbf{\ta{வ}} you copied. Keep that model visible when you copy it again below.

The other four are printed in Tamil in their own lessons, where you were shown them and asked to read nothing. Formal letter construction still begins later, one letter at a time, always spelling a word you already say.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Tamil does not like a blunt goodbye. A bare \textquotedblleft{}I am leaving\textquotedblright{} sounds final in Tamil, even ill-omened, so the everyday farewell is built instead on going \textbf{and coming back} — a promise of return rather than an exit. That whole exchange is a chapter of its own: it needs two verbs you have not met, and you will learn them one at a time.

Which is why \textbf{\ta{வணக்கம்}} is the farewell you already own. It parts as well as it meets, it carries the same respect in both directions, and it commits you to nothing you cannot yet say. Use it when you leave, and the departure exchange will be waiting when its verbs are.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} all five — vaṇakkam · naṉṟi · ām · illai · sari
  \item \emph{Say it:} greet and thank — \textquotedblleft{}vaṇakkam!\textquotedblright{} … \textquotedblleft{}naṉṟi.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Copy:} \textbf{\ta{வ}} once beside the visible model, large and slowly
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say all five words aloud. Which one works both to meet someone and to part from them? (\textbf{\ta{வணக்கம்}}.) Compare your one copied \textbf{\ta{வ}} with the model. Repair one curve if you want, then stop.
